A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their text, equations, proof sections, references, and v2's figures and Appendix A are readable, allowing retained content to be matched despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

before.justification: v1 presents theoretical bounds, proofs, and mathematical distribution constructions, but no original experimental, simulation, or data-analysis outcomes.

after.justification: Section 4 reports original synthetic-data experiments. Appendix A reports CNN prediction histograms and image-interpolation analyses for binary subsets of Fashion MNIST and CIFAR-10.

M1.justification: The clipped, square-loss, lp-regularized minimum-norm ERM procedure is retained. v2 extends the neural models to non-ReLU activations, including tanh/sigmoid architectures in Sections 3.3.2–3.4, without introducing a new optimization or inference algorithm.

E1.justification: From no empirical datasets in v1, v2 adds two-dimensional synthetic classification under weak and hard margins, Fashion MNIST T-shirt versus Pullover, and CIFAR-10 Automobile versus Truck. These introduce synthetic and real-image evaluation coverage.

E2.justification: Neither version reports empirical comparisons against baseline learners. v2's discussions of linear, logistic, kernel, and prior neural classifiers do not constitute evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: v2 introduces sample-size experiments using a fixed (2, 64, 32, 1) ReLU network trained with square loss for 5000 epochs. Appendix A adds binary class selection, CNN training until convergence, test-output histograms, and interclass image interpolation. These are new evaluation protocols.

E4.justification: v2 adds diagnostic analyses of whether margin assumptions appear plausible: synthetic-data prediction histograms and Appendix A's real-data histograms and interpolation case studies. v1 contains no corresponding empirical analyses.

E5.justification: Figures 4 and 6 introduce linear fits to log-log learning curves to estimate convergence exponents. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Figures 4 and 6 newly report decay exponents 0.77 and 1.62 for different weak- and hard-margin synthetic distributions. Appendix A reports more pronounced depletion near zero for Fashion MNIST predictions than CIFAR-10 predictions. The learning-curve axes say validation loss, although their captions call it testing error.

T1.justification: v2 generalizes the error decomposition to parametric classifiers and replaces the L-infinity approximation assumption with distribution-adapted L2 approximation. It replaces assumed polynomial separation with a subanalyticity/KL formulation, adds activation-transfer and tanh/sigmoid results, introduces minimax lower bounds, and supplies four assumption-characterization arguments in Section 6.5.

C1.justification: The abstract and contributions expand the decomposition to general parametric ERM and convergence claims to many activations. They explicitly qualify the ReLU results by distribution-adapted smoothness and add standard-smoothness tanh/sigmoid guarantees and near-minimax claims. The realizable teacher-student exponential-convergence claim is retained.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly acknowledges that A5 is highly nonstandard, discusses approximation obstructions and its incomplete characterization, and distinguishes distribution-adapted guarantees from standard-smoothness results. Sections 3.4 and 5 add limitations concerning optimal rates and explain why extending beyond square loss requires additional calibration arguments.

D1.justification: v2 newly discloses the toy network architecture and epoch budget, plus the appendix CNN's filter counts, kernel sizes, pooling, and fully connected head. These are useful but limited implementation details; optimizer settings, a complete data-generation recipe, and code access are not supplied.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands its theoretical positioning through KL/error-bound literature, tanh approximation, approximation limitations, and minimax constructions, including Bolte et al., De Ryck et al., Safran and Shamir, and Audibert's hypercube framework. Existing activation-approximation literature becomes part of the developed theory rather than only a suggested extension.

P1.justification: The narrative is reorganized from a ReLU-specific setup into general parametric classification followed by neural-network specializations. The abstract, contributions, assumptions discussion, and conclusion are extensively rewritten, while the results and proofs gain a substantially revised subsection structure.

P2.justification: v1 has no figures; v2 introduces ten, covering conceptual margin diagrams, synthetic datasets, prediction histograms, learning curves, and image-interpolation grids. The journal formatting also redesigns the title and author block, headings, running headers, and page layout.

improvement.justification: v2 adds useful applicability discussion, theoretical extensions, and empirical diagnostics. However, it replaces v1's explicit separation assumption with Proposition 1: Section 6.2 invokes a KL inequality in the joint variables (lambda, theta) to assert a theta-only subgradient bound, without establishing that implication and the resulting uniform separation. Figures 4 and 6 also leave validation loss versus testing error ambiguous. These issues affect support for central claims, preventing a reliable net-quality judgment.
